
# Work in progress - pinch of salt!

# Testing on 16th July

After a supercycle change in the SPS, the spill quality and sharing accuracy decrease. During an MD on the 6th of May, we showed that these parameters could largely be recovered by simply trimming the flat-top field to account for the effect of hysteresis. We tried this on an SFT->LHC change, because in that case the hysteretic field is a static offset from the pre-SC change values. However, we actually wanted to compensate for the slow drift of the flat-top observed when switching from LHC->SFT, as this happens over several hours and is generally dealt with by several manual tune trims (see [[Slow Hysteresis Drift]]). I developed simple feed-forward drift compensator (**see [[Drift Corrector]] for detailed slides on this.**) on UCAP which measures the field at a fixed point on the flat-top, finds the delta from that it's meant to be, and then trims the BHYS parameter accordingly to compensate for the hysteretic effect on the next cycle. 

I tested the compensator during [[23-06-2026 MD - Testing Drift Corrector (no beam)]] and [[15-07-2026 MD - Drift Corrector with SHiP]] with beam. The first test proved that the (many) safeguards worked and that the drift could be most eliminated, although there was a slight time-lag due to the one-cycle feed-forward.

During the second test, I turned on the compensator during SFT physics. Dwane kindly played a single LHC cycle which established the hysteresis, and went back to SFT. The compensator worked nicely to counteract the slow drift. You can see in the flat-top field (blue) and the current to the MBIs (magenta). Bear in mind that each point on the graph is one SFTPRO1 flat-top with the relevant quantity measured at a reference point mid-way through the flat-top.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Although the field was compensated nicely, the spill quality (orange) and sharing error (green) acted contrary to expectations from [[06-05-26 MD - Magnetic Calibration, Flat-top Studies]]. In that MD, the spill quality was immediately restored by the flat-top compensation, whereas here it seems to drift unaffected. Likewise in the MD, the sharing error was not entirely fixed by the trim, but here it is a perfect recovery of pre-change levels. Eventually Dwane got a call from the NA complaining about the spill so we turned off the compensation and he did a tune trim as usual.

# Results

Obviously, the observations during the testing did not match the expectations established during the earlier MD. It's not quite clear why the beam parameters can be restored with a dipole trim during an LHC filling SC (as during the MD) but not during SFT physics (during the testing). The only real possibility is that the configuration of the ring during LHC filling is already in some beneficial state which makes a pure dipole trim possible. 

It's possible that this is a tune effect, but QH and QV are actually remarkably stable, both during the MD and during the compensator testing:

# How I Acquired the Data

Most variables come from a reference point on the flat-top (7000ms in cycletime), with the exception of the tune measurements, which come from the very end of the ramp (4350-4450ms). This is because the tune structure is destroyed during debunching at the very start of the flat-top, and it's impossible to get a good tune measurement after this point.

![[Pasted image 20260731120346.png]]

The destruction of the tune structure is visible on the playback, with a very static peak at 0.65 for the remainder of the spill, possibly from the damper.

![[Pasted image 20260731120937.png]]

Due to the fact that Q and I_QF are taken from two different points, they don't correlate with one another. I_QF shows the tune trims on the flat-top, but these don't touch the ramp at all. The tune trims look like this in LSA (one can see that only the extraction region is altered):

![[Pasted image 20260731120421.png]]
